title: Where Next for the UNTOC? The Future of the Palermo Convention
summary: Maya and Daniel examine a briefing from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime on the future of the UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime (UNTOC). They explore the structural delays in the convention's review mechanism, the data gap in the Global South, and the political and financial challenges facing multilateral efforts at COP13.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Welcome back. Today we are digging into a new briefing and event document from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, or GI-TOC. It is titled 'Where Next for the UNTOC? An Inter-Regional Discussion on the Future of the Palermo Convention.' If you work in international diplomacy, cross-border security, law enforcement cooperation, or multilateral policy, this is something you are going to want to pay close attention to.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Right, because the Palermo Convention—which is the UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, or UNTOC—is essentially the bedrock of how countries are supposed to cooperate against illicit networks globally. But this GI-TOC document comes in with a really striking diagnostic right out of the gate.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It really does. The document notes that UNTOC has been in existence for more than 25 years. It is widely recognized as the cornerstone of the United Nations' international response to transnational organized crime. Yet, GI-TOC puts forward a blunt reality: the actual impact of the convention is currently impossible to assess.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Impossible to assess? That is quite a statement for an instrument that has been around for a quarter of a century and has nearly universal adherence. Why is that? What is preventing anyone from measuring whether it actually works?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: According to the briefing, a major driver is the slow progress of its review mechanism. When a treaty like this operates without an effective, functional review mechanism, you do not have the systematic reporting or verified data coming in from state parties to show how the convention is being applied on the ground.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the document points out that this is not just an internal UN observation. It notes that research conducted by academia and civil society in recent years has repeatedly highlighted this severe lack of data, and emphasized that far more concerted efforts are required to enhance implementation.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. And member states themselves have acknowledged this issue during the meetings of the convention's working groups. So you have academia, civil society, and member governments all pointing to the exact same deficit: a critical lack of data and a clear need for coordinated implementation.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: What really jumps out in the text is the geographic imbalance. The document specifically flags that data on the convention's use in the Global South appears to be particularly sporadic. And the consequence of that is severe: it leaves the very countries that need the convention the most without access to the cooperation tools it was built to provide.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: That is a central theme in this briefing. When you consider transnational organized crime, cross-border trafficking networks, and illicit flows, countries in the Global South are often bearing the brunt of the instability and violence. Yet, if the data is sporadic and the convention's operational machinery is not functioning effectively there, those jurisdictions miss out on vital international cooperation tools.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let us unpack what the document says about the review mechanism itself. It states plainly that the review mechanism has been unable to meet its deadlines. What are the specific knock-on effects of those missed deadlines?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: The text lists three very clear consequences. Because the review mechanism is falling behind schedule, countries and societies are left without the information necessary to do three vital things: first, to upgrade their domestic criminalization frameworks; second, to upgrade their international cooperation frameworks; and third, to access capacity-building resources.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Those three elements are essentially the engine of the entire convention, aren't they? If a country cannot assess where its domestic criminal laws fall short of international standards, it cannot update them. If it lacks clear information on cooperation protocols, it cannot execute effective mutual legal assistance or extradition. And without that baseline assessment, how do you even justify or target capacity-building assistance?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Precisely. Capacity building requires a clear understanding of institutional gaps. When the review mechanism stalls, that diagnostic process stops. So states are left flying blind, and civil society and international partners cannot direct technical assistance where it is most urgent.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: So why is this stalling happening? The document addresses the root causes, and it does not shy away from the institutional friction. It mentions the financial crunch facing the United Nations, but it emphasizes that money is only part of the story.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Right. The briefing says explicitly that while the UN financial crunch has no doubt contributed to the challenges facing UNTOC, the convention's challenges have political causes as well as financial causes. That distinction is critical.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: It is, because it is easy in multilateral circles to blame budget shortfalls and hiring freezes for delays. But GI-TOC is reminding everyone that the slow pace of the review mechanism and the hesitancy to share robust operational data often stem from political hesitations among member states.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And that sets the backdrop for why this GI-TOC event is being organized. The occasion is a side event at the 13th Session of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime—COP13. It is scheduled for 21 October 2026, at the Vienna International Centre, running as a hybrid session in room M7.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And look at the stated objective of the event: it is designed to probe, directly within the context of ongoing negotiations at COP13, what states and stakeholders from different regions feel is needed to reinvigorate and reposition the UNTOC, specifically to help states disrupt and dismantle transnational criminal networks.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Notice that phrasing: 'reinvigorate and reposition.' That signals that UNTOC cannot just carry on in maintenance mode. After more than 25 years, with organized criminal syndicates becoming increasingly sophisticated and transnational, the international framework itself has to be actively repositioned if it is going to achieve its ultimate goal of dismantling networks.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: The document also reveals a lot through the coalition of partners and the speaker lineup featured on the flyer. You see logos from GI-TOC, the European Union, the African Union, Canada, Mexico's Secretariat of Foreign Affairs, and the Organization of American States. That is a genuinely inter-regional coalition.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It brings together key diplomatic and regional players from Europe, the Americas, and Africa. And when you look at the speakers listed, you see high-level leadership spanning both policy design and multilateral negotiations.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let us walk through who is on the panel. The session is chaired by Mark Shaw, the Executive Director of the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime. Then we have Ambassador Carl Hallergård, the Permanent Representative of the European Union to the International Organizations in Vienna.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Alongside him is Ambassador José Antonio Zabalgoitia Trejo, Permanent Representative of Mexico to the International Organizations in Vienna. Mexico, of course, has been deeply engaged in international debates on organized crime, arms flows, and illicit markets, especially in Vienna.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Then we have Sandrine Kalisa, Legal Officer with the Criminal, Security and Diplomatic Law Division at Global Affairs Canada. That brings in the technical, legal perspective on how international treaty obligations interact with domestic law and prosecution.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: GI-TOC also features two of its own directors: Cathy Haenlein, Director of Trade and Economic Security, and Ian Tennant, Director of Multilateral Engagement. Having economic security and multilateral diplomacy represented on the panel highlights the dual focus: understanding illicit financial and trade flows, and navigating the diplomatic architecture in Vienna.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the closing remarks are delivered by Ivan Marques, the Secretary for Multidimensional Security at the Organization of American States, the OAS. Having regional bodies like the OAS and the African Union engaged is vital if the goal is truly to bridge that Global South gap the report highlighted.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It goes back directly to what the document identified as the core vulnerability: if the Global South is disconnected from the data gathering, and if countries there are left without access to cooperation tools, the convention fails where it matters most. Having regional organizations like the OAS and the AU in the room is essential for addressing those regional asymmetries.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: So let us connect the dots between the diagnosis and the policy stakes. The document paints a picture of a 25-year-old cornerstone treaty whose impact cannot be evaluated. The review mechanism is missing its deadlines. Member states, academia, and civil society know the data is missing. The UN is in a financial crunch, but political roadblocks are equally to blame.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And meanwhile, the real-world consequence is that domestic laws are not being upgraded, international cooperation frameworks are lagging, and capacity-building resources cannot be effectively deployed. That is the cycle this side event at COP13 is trying to disrupt.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: What do you think is the biggest open question left by this briefing as we look toward COP13 negotiations?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: I think the primary question is whether member states are ready to tackle the political causes of these delays, not just the financial ones. It is relatively easy for states to acknowledge in working group meetings that data is scarce, or to point to UN budget constraints. It is much harder to negotiate solutions that obligate more transparency, streamline review timelines, and ensure that countries across the Global South get genuine operational value out of the convention.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: That is a great point. If the review mechanism is simply a bureaucratic box-ticking exercise that constantly misses its deadlines, it does not help law enforcement or judicial authorities dismantle criminal networks. Repositioning UNTOC means making sure the convention serves actual operational disruption.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. To wrap up our discussion, what to watch next is how these inter-regional discussions unfold in Vienna during COP13. Watch whether the negotiations address the review mechanism's operational backlog, how they plan to close the data gap in the Global South, and whether states are prepared to provide both the political will and the resources needed to make the Palermo Convention truly measurable and effective.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: A vital discussion on the future of global crime fighting. Thanks for listening, and we will see you on the next episode.
